questions.question: Describe any three factors that influence changing rural power.
questions.solution_html:
• Unequal privileges and disabilities: Access to land, education, religious spaces and
  • authority has been unequally distributed.
  • These characteristics have changed substantially. Caste continues through a combination of
  • marriage patterns, social networks, inequalities and political identities rather than through
  • an entirely unchanged traditional order.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning and jati–varna distinction — 2; characteristics — 5;
  • contemporary qualification — 1.
  • 18(b). Describe the risks of digitalisation, including misinformation, surveillance, privacy
  • and the reproduction of inequality.
  • Digitalisation involves the growing use of digital technologies in communication, work,
  • education, governance and everyday life. Alongside its benefits, it produces significant social
  • risks.
  • Misinformation: False or misleading content can circulate rapidly through social media and
  • messaging platforms. It can damage reputations, intensify prejudice and encourage poorly
  • informed decisions. Disinformation refers more specifically to deliberately deceptive
  • content.
  • Surveillance: Governments, companies and other actors can monitor activities through
  • location records, online behaviour, cameras and databases. Excessive monitoring can restrict
  • autonomy and discourage participation or dissent.
  • Privacy risks: Large-scale collection and sharing of personal data can expose individuals to
  • profiling, identity theft, fraud and unwanted disclosure. Consent may be weakened when
  • users cannot understand or meaningfully refuse data practices.
  • Digital inequality: Differences in internet access, devices, affordability and skills affect
  • participation in education, employment and public services. Gender, class, caste, disability,
  • age and location can shape these differences.
  • Reproduction of discrimination: Algorithms trained on unequal or biased data can
  • reproduce disadvantage in recruitment, lending and other decisions.
  • Exclusion from services: Digital-only systems can disadvantage people who lack connectivity,
  • documentation, language support or technical assistance.
  • Example: An online application process may expand convenience while excluding applicants
  • without reliable internet or digital literacy.
  • Addressing these risks requires accessible systems, digital literacy, privacy safeguards,
  • accountable institutions and meaningful alternatives for people facing digital exclusion.
  • Suggested marking: Meaning — 1; four specified risks — 6; example/conclusion — 1.

questions.question: Examine the ways in which factors other than income shape class position.
questions.solution_html:
• How do factors other than income shape class position?
  • • Wealth and property: Land, housing and inherited assets provide security and
  • advantages beyond current earnings.
  • • Occupation and education: Job security, qualifications, skills and authority affect life
  • chances.
  • • Social background and networks: Caste, gender, family connections and access to
  • influential people shape opportunities and mobility.
  • Thus, two people with similar incomes may occupy different class positions because their
  • assets, security and opportunities differ.

questions.question: Describe the central present-day debate about change and equality in the caste system.
questions.solution_html:
• Describe the central present-day debate about change and equality in the caste
  • system.
  • The central debate concerns whether modernisation and democratic change are weakening
  • caste or transforming the ways it operates.
  • • Education, urbanisation, occupational mobility and legal equality have challenged
  • hereditary restrictions.
  • • Yet discrimination, endogamy, unequal resources and caste-based exclusion
  • continue.
  • • Therefore, changes in caste practices do not necessarily indicate the achievement of
  • substantive equality.

questions.question: Examine the ways in which migration can reshape caste and class relations.
questions.solution_html:
• How can migration reshape caste and class relations?
  • • Migration may weaken local caste controls by providing anonymity, new occupations
  • and interaction across caste boundaries.
  • • Earnings and remittances can improve class position and reduce dependence on local
  • landlords or employers.
  • • However, caste networks may continue to organise recruitment, housing and
  • marriage, while insecure employment may reproduce disadvantage.
  • Migration can therefore create mobility while also carrying existing inequalities into new
  • settings.
